cosy-lesson.title: Where You Live Shapes Your Dementia Risk

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Risk – the possibility that something unpleasant or dangerous will happen.

p.em: Example: Living near busy roads can increase the risk of breathing problems.

cosy-blockquote.p: Environment – the surroundings or conditions in which a person, animal, or plant lives.

p.em: Example: A clean environment is very important for our physical health.

cosy-blockquote.p: Brain – the organ inside the head that controls thought, memory, feelings, and activity.

p.em: Example: Reading books and solving puzzles keeps your brain healthy and active.

cosy-blockquote.p: Healthy ≠ Sick – in good physical or mental condition ≠ affected by physical or mental illness.

p.em: Example: Eating fresh vegetables helps you stay healthy, but eating too much sugar can make you sick.
Example: Scientists analyzed a massive amount of medical data for this study.

cosy-blockquote.p: Neighborhood – a district or community within a town or city.

p.em: Example: There is a very friendly atmosphere in our small neighborhood.

cosy-blockquote.p: Discover – find unexpectedly or during a search.

p.em: Example: Researchers discover new facts about human biology every single day.

cosy-blockquote.p: Study – a detailed investigation and analysis of a subject or situation.

p.em: Example: The medical study lasted for more than ten years.

cosy-blockquote.p: Protect – keep safe from harm or injury.

p.em: Example: Wearing a helmet helps protect your head when riding a bicycle.

cosy-blockquote.p: Influence – have an effect on the character, development, or behavior of someone or something.

p.em: Example: Your friends can have a big influence on your daily choices.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
According to the article, how can our surrounding environment influence our daily health?
★ Do you prefer living in a bustling big city or a quiet countryside town?

Does the text say that busy city roads increase the risk of brain problems?
★ How easily can you find a public park or green garden near your current home?

Why is it important for scientists to do a massive study on brain health?
★ Do you feel that your local neighborhood is safe and pleasant for walking?

According to the text, what simple activities can help protect our brain as we get older?
★ How does the amount of natural sunlight in your home affect your daily mood?

How does the study show that a green neighborhood feels better and keeps us active?
★ What is your favorite way to stay active and get fresh air on the weekends?

Why do some cities want to build green parks to keep people healthy ≠ sick?
★ Is there a lot of traffic noise or air pollution where you currently live?

According to researchers, what kind of habits keep a human brain active and fit?
★ Did your childhood home have a garden or big trees nearby where you played?

What details does the study give about the number of senior citizens analyzed?
★ How often do you interact with or greet your neighbors in your daily routine?

How did the scientific team discover the link between where we live and our memory?
★ What is the most peaceful and quiet place you have visited in your region?

How does the article describe the ways environmental factors influence our daily choices?
★ Do you think the layout of a city can encourage people to lead healthier lives?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
In the future, will cities redesign every neighborhood to put a forest near our homes?
★ Would you move to a smaller, quieter town if it guaranteed better brain health as you age?

As our understanding of this discovery develops, we will use smart devices to track how much air pollution enters our brain every day.
★ Do you think future cities will be designed with mandatory green parks on every block?

If certain trees can reduce our risk of brain disease, will cities plant them on every street?
★ Would you support a complete ban on cars in city centers to reduce noise and pollution?

In the future, will doctors tell us to walk in the forest to stay healthy ≠ sick?
★ Should employers offer outdoor green-working hours to prevent mental fatigue?

As our understanding of this discovery develops, architects will construct massive green gardens inside apartment buildings.
★ Would you use a map app that recommends walking routes based on clean air and low noise?

If clean air can protect our memory, will we buy houses based only on clean air?
★ Do you think real estate values should be determined by environmental health indexes?

If green parks help our health, will governments build more parks in every city environment?
★ Would you live in a futuristic eco-commune with shared gardens and no private cars?

As our understanding of this discovery develops, every medical study will include spatial maps of where patients live.
★ What is the most important change you would make to improve your current neighborhood?

If bright city lights influence how we sleep, should cities turn off street lights after midnight?
★ Do you think the next generation will be healthier physically because of smart cities?

If smelling green trees is good for our memory, what else will scientists discover?
★ How do you personally protect your peace of mind and mental quiet in a busy world?

ul.li: Incorrect: I am live in a green city. → Correct: I live in a green city. ((Verb conjugation: do not use the auxiliary 'am' with the active verb 'live'.))
Incorrect: He is more healthy than me. → Correct: He is healthier than me. ((Comparative suffix: 'healthy' becomes 'healthier'.))
Incorrect: There is many parks here. → Correct: There are many parks here. ((Plural agreement: use 'are' when talking about multiple parks.))
